Part 1 · Marks

Four marks, four promises

These goods are ours.

Trademark

One business marks its own goods, so buyers can tell them apart from others.

Textbook examples: MAMA, Wai Wai, Yum Yum

This service is ours.

Service mark

The same idea, for a service instead of a product.

Textbook examples: a bank or an airline

This passed the test.

Certification mark

Others may use it only when they meet the owner’s set criteria. Nothing more is promised.

Textbook illustration: Shell Shuan Shim

We are members.

Collective mark

Shared by the members of a group, such as a co-op. Non-members may not use it.

Textbook example: SCG · like a co-op logo on members’ goods

Examples as given in the textbook, p. 91: illustrations, not statements about legal registration.

Recap · who uses it, what it says

One business,
one sign

Trademark

Used by its owner, on its goods

These goods come from us.

Service mark

Used by its owner, for its services

This service comes from us.

One name.
One business behind it.

Many users,
one sign

Certification mark

The way in: meet the criteria

Used by any business that meets the criteria set by the mark’s owner

This met the stated criteria.

Collective mark

The way in: be a member

Used by members of the group, and only by members

This comes from one of our members.

All four answer who.
Which sign answers where?

Part 2 · Geographical indications

A GI ties quality
to a place

A geographical indication (GI) is a sign on products from a specific place. Their quality, reputation or characteristics are due to that origin.

NatureRaw materials and environment
PeopleSkills and methods
One place

Thai tamarind: pod, shell, pulp, fibres and seeds. Illustrative only; the producing province is not verified. Photo: Stanhopea · CC BY 2.0 DE · cropped

Shows up in the product asQuality · Reputation · Characteristics

Nature and people meet in one place.
That link is what the sign protects.

Definition paraphrased from WIPO, Frequently Asked Questions: Geographical Indications.

Case study · a Thai GI

Read the label.
Then turn it over.

Place + product = one GI name.

The back gives the reasons: nature and people, in this one place.

Khao Kho, Phetchabun province. A landscape of the province; not presented as a tamarind orchard. Photo: Love Krittaya · public domain · cropped, darkened

Side by side

Two signs, two questions

Both are signs that buyers rely on. They do different jobs; neither one is “better”.

Trademark

answers: who?

Which business stands behind the product
Its owner, and anyone the owner licenses
Often an invented or arbitrary name
Yes. It can be sold or licensed to anyone, anywhere

Geographical indication

answers: where?

Which place it comes from, and the quality tied to that place
Producers in the area who follow the agreed standards
Usually the name of the place
No. It cannot be licensed to producers outside the place
Tells
you
Who may

The
name
Can it
move?
Quick check 1A noodle company moves its factory to another province. Can it keep its brand name?
Quick check 2A farm outside Phetchabun grows very sweet tamarind. May it use the GI name?

Yes. The mark follows the business.

No. The name belongs to the place and its standards.

Comparison paraphrased from WIPO, FAQ: Geographical Indications. Photos: shelf by 維基小霸王 (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Khao Kho, Phetchabun, by Love Krittaya (public domain); both cropped and darkened.

Takeaway

So, which is which?

Brand tells who.
Place tells where.

Say your answer out loud. Then turn the labels over.

A trademark points to a business. A GI points to a place, and to the quality tied to it.
